items.body: China And St. Augustine - Gavekal Research RESEARCH Gavekal Research Gavekal Dragonomics Gavekal-IS Gavekal Technologies Gavekal Technologies: Briefing Gavekal Technologies: Chips Gavekal Technologies: New Energy Videos AUTHORS Gavekal Research Louis-Vincent Gave Charles Gave Anatole Kaletsky August Gudmundsson Cedric Gemehl Pierre Gave Rohan Daswani Simon Pritchard Tan Kai Xian Tom Holland Tom Miller Udith Sikand Will Denyer Gavekal Dragonomics Andrew Batson Arthur Kroeber Christopher Beddor Ernan Cui Thomas Gatley Tilly Zhang Wei He Xiaoxi Zhang Gavekal-IS Didier Darcet Gavekal Technologies AJ Cortese Arthur Kroeber Damien Ma Huang Shichan Laila Khawaja Tom Hancock REGIONS America China Europe Asia DASHBOARD Gavekal Dashboard Personal Dashboard EVENTS Login China And St. Augustine Louis-Vincent Gave Gavekal Research | 23 Oct 2026 Back in the summer of 2015, the Chinese government decided that equity markets had risen too far, too fast. The rug was pulled from under margin lending and various restrictions were put in place that brought the unfolding raging equity bull market to an abrupt end. By January 2024, the Chinese government reversed course and decided that Chinese equity prices had fallen far enough. Beijing intervened in the market (see Chinese Policies And Chinese Equities ) and put a floor under domestic markets. Equities duly rallied, delivering very solid returns for 2024 and 2025. However, over the past year, Chinese equity market returns have been fairly dismal. In fact, Chinese equity markets have now fallen for 10 consecutive weeks, a feat they had never achieved before. This in spite of the fact that (a) excitement over all things “artificial intelligence” has been a key driver of global equity market performance and that (b) China is one of the few countries outside of the US actually registering notable gains on the AI front. In short, Chinese equities have had a very disappointing month, quarter, year-to-date and 12 months and what had been steady outperformance has now melted away like snow in the sun. items.author: Michael Pettis
items.title_en: The Plaza Accord and Its Relevance for China | Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
items.title_zh: The Plaza Accord and Its Relevance for China | Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
items.summary_en: The Plaza Accord was not an externally imposed punishment of Japan but part of a broader restructuring that Japanese economists and policymakers themselves recognized was necessary. Its effects were undermined, however, when Tokyo responded to the resulting slowdown with policies that exacerbated investment, credit expansion, and the very imbalances the adjustment was intended to resolve.

items.body: Commentary China Financial Markets Beijing’s Three Options: Unemployment, Debt, or Wealth Transfers China’s debt problems have emerged so much more rapidly and severely this year than in the past that a growing number of analysts believe that this may be the year that China’s economy breaks. There is no question that China will have a difficult adjustment, but it is likely to take the form of a long process rather than a sudden crisis. Michael Pettis

Ben King Listen Power is at the center of Americans’ lives. It lets us cool our homes, keeps them lit, and charges our electronics. But the more things we plug into our aging power grid, the more strained it becomes. And electricity use in the U.S. is rising for the first time in more than a decade. What happens when our grid can’t keep up? NPR’s 1A show sits down with a panel of experts, including Rhodium director Ben King.
